outputs.L1:
Tulsidas, the poet, was wandering deep in thought beside the Ganges, in that lonely place where the dead are consigned to the flames. There he found a woman seated at the feet of her husband’s corpse, adorned brightly, as though for a wedding.

When she saw him, she rose, bowed, and said, “Permit me, Master, with your blessing, to follow my husband to heaven.”

“Why such haste, my daughter?” asked Tulsidas. “Is not this earth also His who made heaven?”

“For heaven I do not long,” said the woman. “I want my husband.”

Tulsidas smiled and said to her, “Go back to your home, my child. Before the month is over, you will find your husband.”

The woman returned, filled with joyful hope. Each day, Tulsidas came to her and offered her lofty thoughts to contemplate, until her heart was filled to the brim with divine love.

When the month had scarcely passed, her neighbours came to her and asked, “Woman, have you found your husband?”

The widow smiled and said, “I have.”

Eagerly they asked, “Where is he?”

“In my heart is my lord, one with me,” said the woman.
outputs.L2:
Tulsidas, the poet, was walking alone beside the Ganges, lost in contemplation, near the deserted place where the dead were cremated. There he came upon a woman seated by the body of her deceased husband, dressed brightly as though prepared for marriage.

When she noticed him, she stood up, bowed respectfully, and said, “Master, allow me, with your blessing, to go with my husband to heaven.”

“My daughter,” Tulsidas asked, “why are you in such haste? Does not the One who created heaven also possess this earth?”

“I do not desire heaven,” the woman replied. “I desire my husband.”

Tulsidas smiled and told her, “Return to your house, my child. Before this month ends, you will find your husband.”

Filled with joyful expectation, the woman went home. Each day Tulsidas visited her and guided her toward noble and spiritual thoughts, until her heart overflowed with divine love.

When the month had nearly passed, her neighbours came and asked, “Woman, have you found your husband?”

The widow smiled and answered, “Yes, I have.”

They asked eagerly, “Where is he?”

“My lord is within my heart,” she said. “He is united with me.”

One day, Tulsidas encountered a widow on the banks of the Ganges. She was preparing to follow her dead husband to heaven, believing that this was the only way she could remain with him. Seeing her grief and determination, Tulsidas spoke to her with compassion and asked her what she truly desired.

The widow replied that she had no wish for heaven itself. She did not long for heavenly pleasures, rewards, or glory. Her only desire was to be with her husband. Without him, she felt that life had lost all meaning.

Tulsidas gently urged her to return home instead of giving herself up to despair. He assured her that if she followed his guidance, she would find her husband within a month. Though uncertain, the widow trusted his words and agreed to go back.

Each day, Tulsidas guided her in prayer, remembrance, and devotion. He helped her turn her sorrow inward, transforming her grief into a deeper love. Gradually, her heart became filled with divine love, and her sense of separation began to fade.

By the end of the month, the widow experienced a profound realization. She understood that her husband had not truly been lost to her. He lived within her heart, united with her in the presence of the Divine. What she had sought outside herself, she discovered within: a love that death could not destroy.
outputs.L4:
When Tulsidas was traveling from village to village, singing the name of Rama and teaching the path of devotion, he came one evening to a place heavy with sorrow. A man had died that day, and his body had been carried to the cremation ground. Beside the funeral pyre stood his young widow, dressed in the garments of mourning, her face pale with grief and resolve. The villagers whispered that she had decided to die with her husband, believing that life without him had no meaning.

Tulsidas saw the pain in her eyes and approached her gently. He did not scold her, nor did he speak harshly against her despair. Instead, he asked, “Daughter, whom do you love so deeply that you wish to follow him into the flames?”

“My husband,” she replied, weeping. “He was my life. Without him, I am empty.”

Tulsidas looked at her with compassion and said, “If he was truly your life, then he cannot be destroyed by fire. What you loved in him was not merely the body that lies before you. The body is made of dust and returns to dust, but love belongs to the soul. If your love is true, then seek him where love lives—not in the flames, but in the heart.”

The widow trembled. Her grief was so powerful that she could hardly understand him, but his words carried a strange peace. Tulsidas asked her to wait for one month before taking any final step. “Give me thirty days,” he said. “Each day, come and listen to the name of Rama. If, after that, you still believe there is no life for you, then decide as your heart commands.”

The villagers were silent. The widow, exhausted by sorrow, agreed.

From the next morning onward, she came to Tulsidas. At first she sat apart, her head lowered, unable to speak. Tulsidas recited verses, sang hymns, and spoke to her about the eternal nature of the soul. He explained that all earthly relationships are sacred when they lead the heart toward God, but none of them are meant to end in destruction. Love, he told her, is not possession of another person’s body; it is recognition of the divine presence within them.

Day after day, he guided her gently. He asked her to remember her husband not with the cry, “He is gone,” but with the prayer, “May the love I knew through him lead me closer to the Eternal.” He encouraged her to repeat the name of Rama whenever grief rose like a storm within her. At first the name came from her lips mechanically, mixed with tears. But slowly, the sound began to steady her breath. The moments of unbearable anguish grew shorter. In their place came a quiet tenderness.

Tulsidas also taught her to serve. “If you wish to honor your husband,” he said, “let your life become an offering. Feed the hungry in his memory. Comfort those who suffer. Let the love you felt for one person widen until it embraces all beings.” The widow began to help in small ways. She brought water to the old, food to children, and flowers to the shrine. Each act softened her grief, not because she forgot her husband, but because she felt his memory becoming part of something larger and holier.

As the days passed, she noticed a change within herself. Earlier, every memory of her husband had pierced her like a thorn. Now those same memories glowed like lamps. She could hear his voice in her mind without collapsing into despair. She could remember his kindness and feel gratitude instead of only loss. She began to understand what Tulsidas had meant: the love between them had not been burned away by death. It had entered her heart more deeply.

On the last day of the month, she came to Tulsidas with tears in her eyes, but they were no longer the tears of hopelessness.

“Master,” she said, “when my husband died, I thought my life had ended. I wanted to enter the fire because I believed he was outside me, lost forever. But now I see that what I truly loved in him was never separate from me. His body has gone, but his love lives in my heart. And beyond even that love, I feel the presence of Rama, who dwells in every soul.”

Tulsidas smiled and blessed her. “Now you have understood. Human love becomes complete when it leads us to divine love. The one you mourned has become a doorway to God. Do not throw away the life through which such realization has come. Live, and let your heart be a temple.”

The widow bowed before him. She did not return to the funeral pyre. Instead, she chose a life of devotion, remembrance, and service. Her grief did not vanish as though it had never existed, but it was transformed. What had once been a wound became a sacred space within her. She carried her husband not as a chain binding her to death, but as a living presence in the heart, joined with the divine love that unites all beings.

Thus Tulsidas showed that despair can be turned toward devotion, and that love, when purified by spiritual understanding, does not end in separation. It becomes inner union, strength, and peace.

Tulsidas, one of the most revered poets and saints of India, is remembered for his deep devotion to Lord Rama and for composing the *Ramcharitmanas*, a beloved retelling of the Ramayana in Awadhi. His words brought spiritual wisdom closer to ordinary people, allowing them to connect with faith through simple yet powerful poetry.

The sacred river Ganges is often associated with devotion, purity, and the spiritual life of India. Many saints, pilgrims, and seekers have found inspiration on her banks. She flows not only as a river but also as a symbol of grace, carrying centuries of prayers, stories, and traditions.

In the world of Tulsidas, the Ganges represents more than water; she reflects the divine compassion that cleanses the heart and guides the soul toward truth. Just as his verses continue to inspire millions, the Ganges continues her eternal journey, reminding people of faith, renewal, and the timeless bond between nature and spirituality.

counterfactuals.prompt: Retell a short spiritual parable about Tulsidas meeting a widow by the Ganges who wants to follow her dead husband, ending with her finding him in her heart.
counterfactuals.output:
By the banks of the Ganges, as the evening lamps began to tremble on the water, Tulsidas saw a young widow weeping beside her husband’s funeral pyre.

“Holy one,” she said, “my husband has gone ahead of me. Tell me how I may follow him.”

Tulsidas looked at her with deep compassion. “If you truly wish to find him,” he said, “then sit here by the river and call his name—not with your lips alone, but with your whole heart.”

So she sat through the night, repeating his name through tears. At first she saw only smoke, ashes, and the dark river flowing past. But slowly her grief became still. Her breath softened. Her heart opened.

Then, in the silence, she felt a warmth within her—not the warmth of fire, but of love that had never left. She understood: the body had gone to ash, but the love she sought was not across the river, not in death, not in the pyre.

It was shining quietly within her own heart.

When dawn came, Tulsidas returned.

“Did you find your husband?” he asked.

The widow bowed, her face peaceful.

“Yes,” she said. “I looked for him in the flames, but I found him in my heart.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a brief story in a poetic, old-fashioned style about Tulsidas persuading a grieving woman not to commit sati and teaching her divine love.
counterfactuals.output:
In the days when the dust of the road was sweet with pilgrims’ songs, Goswami Tulsidas came to a village by the river, where the smoke of funeral fires hung like a sorrowful veil.

There he beheld a young widow, pale as moonlight upon ashes, walking toward her husband’s pyre. Her kinsfolk wept, yet none stayed her feet; for grief had bound her heart with iron cords, and the world seemed emptied of all tenderness.

Tulsidas, moved with compassion, stood before her and raised his hand.

“Daughter,” said he, in a voice gentle as the evening bell, “whither goest thou in such haste?”

“To my lord,” she answered, her eyes fixed upon the flames. “Without him, this life is but a broken lute.”

Then the saint spoke: “Nay, child. The body is a garment worn for a little while; love is not burned with wood, nor buried with dust. If thou wouldst seek thy true Lord, turn thy heart to Rama, whose mercy outlives death and whose name is a bridge across the dark river.”

She trembled. “But my heart is ashes.”

“Then sow therein the name of God,” said Tulsidas. “From ashes also the sacred fire is born. Thy husband was dear to thee; let that love become a lamp, not a flame to consume thee. Live, and let thy tears be offerings. Serve the poor, comfort the lonely, and remember that the Lord dwelleth in every wounded breast.”

At these words, the woman’s steps faltered. The fire before her roared, but within her another fire awakened—soft, steady, and deathless.

She turned away from the pyre and fell at the saint’s feet. Tulsidas lifted her, saying, “Rise, mother. No soul is widowed that has found the Beloved Eternal.”

And from that day, she lived not as one bereft, but as one illumined; and upon her lips, morning and night, blossomed the holy name: “Rama, Rama.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a prose passage set at a cremation ground by the Ganges, featuring the poet Tulsidas, a newly widowed woman, and a lesson about love becoming inward and spiritual.
counterfactuals.output:
At Manikarnika, where the Ganges moved like a long breath beside the steps, the fires did not sleep.

Smoke climbed into the evening, blue and gold, carrying sandalwood, ghee, and grief. Bells rang from a temple above the ghats; priests murmured syllables older than memory. Dogs threaded the shadows. The river received ashes with the same quiet with which it received flowers.

Near one newly lit pyre sat a woman in a white sari, her bangles broken, the red in the parting of her hair washed away. She was very young. The flames that held her husband rose and fell before her eyes, and each time the wood cracked she trembled, as if something in her own body had split.

Tulsidas, old and slight, wrapped in a plain cloth, had come down to the river after dusk. He stood for some time without speaking. His face, lined by years of recitation and wandering, reflected the firelight softly. At last he sat a little distance from the widow, close enough that she would know he was there, not so close that her sorrow would feel crowded.

“They have taken him from me,” she said, though no one had asked.

Tulsidas lowered his gaze to the river. “The river takes nothing,” he answered. “It carries.”

She turned toward him with eyes reddened by smoke and weeping. “What can be carried when the body is burning?”

“The body returns to the elements,” he said. “But love is not wood for the pyre.”

She laughed once, bitterly. “Do not speak to me of love, Baba. Love was his voice in the courtyard. Love was his hand on the door at evening. Love was the place beside me on the mat. Look there—” She pointed to the fire. “That is what love has become.”

Tulsidas watched the flames lean in the wind. For a while he said nothing, and in his silence her anger found no wall to strike.

Then he said, “When I was young, I too thought love lived only in a face, a form, a nearness. I clung to it as a drowning man clings to a reed. But what is seen can be lost. What is touched can be taken away. The heart suffers because it builds its house on the bank of a changing river.”

The woman covered her face. “Then are we wrong to love?”

“No,” said Tulsidas gently. “We are wrong only when we believe love ends at the skin.”

The fire brightened. Sparks rose like small, brief stars.

“Your husband’s voice has ceased outside you,” he continued, “but the tenderness it awakened need not die. Let it turn inward. Let it become prayer. Let the warmth you gave one person widen until it touches all beings. This is not forgetting him. This is allowing love to grow beyond the doorway where you last saw him.”

She listened, though her shoulders still shook.

“The world teaches us love by giving us a form,” Tulsidas said. “A mother, a child, a friend, a husband. We begin there because the heart is small and needs a lamp it can see. But the lamp is not the sun. When the form is taken, we are invited—painfully, unwillingly—to seek the flame that was shining through it.”

The widow looked back at the pyre. The fierce outline of her grief did not soften, but it became still.

“How can I pray,” she whispered, “when I am angry with God?”

“Then offer the anger,” said Tulsidas. “Offer the emptiness. Offer the questions. The Lord does not ask first for sweetness. He asks for truth.”

Below them, a priest descended the steps and scattered marigolds into the darkening Ganges. The flowers drifted past the burning grounds, bright and fragile upon the black water.

Tulsidas began to chant, not loudly, but with a steadiness that seemed to enter the spaces between the crackle of fire and the hush of the river. The name of Rama moved on his breath like a bead passing through fingers.

The widow did not join him. She only sat, palms open on her knees.

But after a long time, when the pyre had settled and the moon had risen pale over Kashi, she lifted one hand to her heart—not to clutch at it, but to feel within it for something that had not burned. There, beneath the ash of loss, beneath the wild cry of absence, was a small warmth.

It was not yet consolation. It was not yet peace.

But it was love, no longer standing outside her in mortal form, beginning its difficult journey inward.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you compose a Rabindranath Tagore-like moral tale where Tulsidas blesses a widow who asks to join her husband in heaven, but she later realizes he lives within her heart?
counterfactuals.output:
At the edge of Kashi, where the Ganga moved like a hymn half-remembered by the earth, there lived a young widow named Kamala.

Her husband had died in the spring, when the mango blossoms were still pale and fragrant. Since then, the world had seemed to her like a lamp with its flame blown out. The river shone, the temple bells rang, the parrots cried from the neem trees—but all these things came to her as if from very far away.

One morning she heard that the saint Tulsidas was sitting beneath a banyan tree near the ghats, speaking to those who came with sorrow. Kamala wrapped her white sari closely about her and went to him.

The saint’s face was calm, like the sky after rain. Around him sat merchants, mendicants, children, and old women with brass pots at their hips. When Kamala approached, the crowd grew silent, for grief has a dignity before which even curiosity lowers its eyes.

She bowed and said, “Master, my husband has gone to heaven. Bless me, so that I may join him there.”

Tulsidas looked at her for a long while. The Ganga murmured at the steps below.

“My child,” he said gently, “if I bless you to find your husband, will you accept the road by which the Lord leads you?”

“I will,” said Kamala. “Only let me find him.”

Then Tulsidas lifted his hand and blessed her.

“May you find him where love has hidden him.”

Kamala returned home with a strange peace, yet also with impatience. Each night she looked at the stars and wondered which one was the doorway to her husband’s dwelling. Each dawn she rose disappointed to find herself still among the living.

Days passed.

One afternoon, an old woman from the neighboring house fell ill. No one was there to bring water from the well. Kamala, who had long kept herself apart from the village, heard the woman calling and went to her. She brought water, cooled her forehead, and sat beside her through the night.

As the old woman slept, she murmured, “Daughter, your hands are like my dead son’s hands. He too was gentle.”

At those words Kamala’s heart trembled. She remembered how her husband had tended a wounded calf once, whispering to it as if it were a frightened child.

The next day a hungry boy came to her door. Kamala gave him the rice she had saved for herself. When he smiled, a sudden light filled her eyes, for in that smile she saw the same kindness that had once shone from her husband’s face.

Later, in the rains, a traveler slipped in the mud outside her courtyard. Kamala helped him rise and washed the clay from his feet. As she did so, she heard within herself her husband’s voice, not as memory, but as presence:

“Where compassion is, there I am.”

Kamala sat still.

The rain fell from the eaves like strings of pearls. The little tulsi plant in her courtyard bent under the drops and rose again.

That evening she went back to Tulsidas.

“Master,” she said, with tears that were no longer bitter, “I asked you to send me to heaven. But you sent me among the sorrowful.”

Tulsidas smiled. “And did you not find what you sought?”

Kamala placed her hand upon her breast.

“I searched the sky for my husband,” she said, “but he was living here, in the love he left behind. When I serve, he speaks. When I give, he smiles. When I forgive, he comes near.”

The saint bowed his head.

“Then the blessing has borne fruit,” he said. “Heaven is not reached by fleeing the world, but by discovering the eternal in love. Those whom we truly love do not vanish into distance. They become the lamp by which we learn to see others.”

From that day, Kamala no longer called herself empty. She lived simply, but her house became a place where the weary found water, the hungry found food, and the grieving found a listener.

And the villagers would say, “She is a widow.”

But the children, who knew better, said, “No. Her heart is full.”

For love, when it is true, does not end at the funeral fire. It changes its dwelling—from the hand we held to the hand we extend, from the voice we heard to the kindness we speak, from one beloved form to the whole wide world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an inspirational Indian saint story: Tulsidas encounters a widow dressed for her funeral rites, counsels her for a month, and she discovers her husband is one with her in her heart.
counterfactuals.output:
## The Lamp in the Heart: A Story of Tulsidas

In the holy city of Kashi, where the Ganga flowed like a silver prayer and temple bells awakened the dawn, the saint Tulsidas spent his days singing the name of Shri Rama.

One morning, as he walked toward the river with his mala in hand, he saw a small crowd moving silently through the narrow lane. At the center walked a young widow, dressed in the solemn garments of funeral rites. Her eyes were dry, but not because she had no grief—rather, because grief had gone deeper than tears.

Her husband had died suddenly, and in the darkness of her sorrow she had decided that her own life had ended with his.

Tulsidas stopped before her.

“Daughter,” he said gently, “where are you going?”

She bowed her head. “Maharaj, my husband has left this world. What remains for me here?”

Tulsidas looked at her with deep compassion. “If your husband has truly left you, then search for him. But do not search in fire, ashes, or despair. Come to my hut for one month. If after that you still feel he is nowhere to be found, I will not stop you from choosing your path.”

The people murmured. The widow hesitated.

There was something in the saint’s voice—not command, but kindness; not argument, but truth. At last she agreed.

For the next month, she came to Tulsidas every morning.

On the first day, she wept.

Tulsidas let her weep. He did not hurry her grief. He only said, “Tears are also a form of prayer when they fall before God.”

On the second day, he asked her to speak of her husband—not of his death, but of his life.

She spoke of his laughter, his honesty, the way he fed stray cows, the way he brought her flowers during spring, the way he never ate until he had asked whether she had eaten.

Tulsidas listened and said, “See, he is not only in the body that has gone. He is in every kindness that remains.”

On another day, he gave her a small lamp and said, “Light this before Rama each evening. Then sit quietly and ask: ‘What did my husband love in me? What goodness did he awaken in my heart?’”

She did so.

At first, there was only pain. Then slowly, memories came—not like knives, but like soft lamps in a dark room.

She remembered how her husband had encouraged her to read sacred verses. She remembered how he had once said, “Your heart is your greatest temple.” She remembered the devotion they had shared, the prayers they had whispered together, the dreams they had offered to God.

Day by day, Tulsidas taught her from the Ramayana.

“Did Sita live only because Rama was beside her?” he asked. “No. Even in separation, Rama lived in her heart. Love is not destroyed by distance. True love becomes inner strength.”

The widow listened.

The saint continued, “The body is like a clay pot. One day it breaks. But the space inside the pot does not die—it joins the vast sky. Your husband’s body has returned to dust, but the love, dharma, and devotion you shared are not dead. They have entered your heart.”

A month passed.

On the final morning, the widow came to Tulsidas with calm eyes. She was no longer dressed for death. She wore simple white, and in her hands she carried the little lamp he had given her.

Tulsidas asked, “Daughter, have you found your husband?”

She bowed, tears shining now with peace.

“Yes, Maharaj,” she said. “I searched for him in the place where his body was taken, and I found only sorrow. I searched for him in my memories, and I found sweetness. I searched for him in prayer, and I found strength. But when I searched in my own heart, I discovered he had never left me.”

Tulsidas smiled.

“Then live,” he said, “not as one abandoned, but as one entrusted with love. Let your life become a lamp lit from his love and offered to Rama.”

From that day forward, the widow served the poor, fed pilgrims, and sang the name of God. People who came to comfort her found themselves comforted instead.

And whenever someone asked how she had survived such grief, she would place her hand upon her heart and say:

“Love does not end when the body falls. The one we truly love becomes one with us—quietly, deeply, in the temple of the heart.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
